summary: A note from the Network Information Center on its enterprise phone service, set up in 1971 so ARPANET sites could call the NIC with tolls billed to the NIC. It attaches a list of numbers and explains that a single 800 number would cost far more, about $2200 per month versus about $800. It updates two earlier NIC documents.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC lists Enterprise and Zenith phone numbers that ARPANET sites could use to call the NIC. It compares their monthly cost with the cost of one 800 number.

subtitle: A current list of phone arrangements for calling the Network Information Center.

tldr.problem: The NIC maintained phone arrangements for network sites and needed to share the current numbers and service details.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists Enterprise and Zenith numbers by site and explains why the NIC did not consolidate them into one 800 number.
tldr.outcome: It provides the list, asks for user feedback, and invites sites without arrangements to request them.

facts.label: Estimated monthly cost of one 800 number

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 511's status as Unknown. This RFC records phone arrangements for the NIC and network sites.

sections.title: Phone Service to the NIC
sections.content: The Network Information Center had arranged phone service for network sites, with tolls billed to the NIC. This RFC updates the list of Enterprise and Zenith numbers and says the list is also available online through LOCATOR.
sections.plainLanguage: Sites could call the NIC using special phone arrangements. The RFC publishes an updated list of numbers.

sections.title: Why Not One 800 Number
sections.content:
The NIC considered consolidating the service to one 800 number but says it would cost more. Enterprise arrangements had to be made separately for each prefix, not just each area code.

The RFC estimates the current arrangement at about $800 per month and one 800 number at about $2,200 per month.
sections.plainLanguage: The NIC says a single 800 number would be more expensive than the existing arrangements. Separate phone arrangements were needed for prefixes.

sections.title: Numbers and After-Hours Calls
sections.content:
The RFC lists sites and their Enterprise or Zenith numbers and invites connected sites without an Enterprise number to request one. It also says an answering service had been arranged for calls received from 5 p.m. to 8 a.m.

The answering service was intended to provide information about NIC operations outside the hours when its full staff was present.
sections.plainLanguage: The table tells sites which number to call. An answering service was intended to give NIC status information outside staffed hours.
